sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: Sell limited inventory when millions of users arrive together. The example offers 10,000 units at a fixed sale time.
Successful reservations and purchases must never exceed inventory. A reservation temporarily holds a unit while payment completes.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: Users can view the sale product, price, and sale window.
Users can reserve an available unit for a limited checkout period.
Users with valid reservations can pay for their units. General catalog search, shipping, returns, and sale administration are outside the scope.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: Prevent overselling even when many requests compete for the same unit.
Handle millions of arrivals within seconds. Give users a fair opportunity to reach the reservation path.
A failed payment must not hold inventory forever. Keep reservation state consistent when payment results or cleanup arrive late.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: Product stores sale details, price, timing, and inventory. User identifies the buyer.
Reservation records the user, product, expiry, and current claim state. Later designs associate each claim with an individual unit.
Purchase links a reservation to payment amount and status. It distinguishes pending, completed, and failed purchases.
A later admission token proves that the Waiting Room Service allowed the user to attempt a reservation. It does not reserve inventory.

sections.title: API
points: GET /products/{id} returns sale details. Any displayed inventory count can change before the buyer reserves a unit.
POST /products/{id}/reservations attempts a temporary claim. A successful response includes the reservation ID and expiry.
POST /reservations/{id}/purchases starts checkout. GET /purchases/{id} lets the buyer recover the final result after a lost response.
Check sale timing, reservation ownership, state, and expiry on the server. A client countdown cannot authorize a purchase.

sections.title: 1) Browse and reserve
points: The basic read path is client, API Gateway, Sale Service, then PostgreSQL. The Sale Service returns the product record.
Initially, one transaction conditionally decrements the product inventory count and inserts a Reservation. Both changes must commit together.
The reservation has an explicit expiry. A cron job marks expired reservations and restores inventory in another transaction.
The reservation response grants a temporary claim. Do not keep a database transaction open while the buyer enters payment details.

flows.title: Reserve inventory in the baseline design
steps: The client requests a reservation through the API Gateway.
The Sale Service starts a short PostgreSQL transaction and checks that the sale is active.
It conditionally decrements available inventory and creates the buyer's Reservation with an expiry.
The transaction commits both changes together. A failed claim must not create a reservation.
The service returns the reservation ID and checkout deadline. The later waiting room limits who can reach this path.

sections.title: 2) Complete payment
points: The Sale Service validates the reservation and creates a pending Purchase. It creates a Stripe PaymentIntent and returns the client secret.
The client submits payment details directly to Stripe. A verified webhook later reports the result to the Sale Service.
Success updates Purchase and Reservation together. Define the policy for payment success after expiry; a late callback cannot take a reassigned unit.
The buyer polls Purchase status until it is final. A processor response alone does not prove that the local purchase has committed.

flows.title: Convert a valid reservation into a purchase
steps: The client requests checkout for its reservation.
The Sale Service verifies the claim and saves a pending Purchase.
It creates a Stripe PaymentIntent and returns the client secret to the client.
The client submits payment details directly to Stripe and confirms payment.
Stripe sends a webhook with the result. The Sale Service verifies it and applies the allowed purchase and reservation transition.
The client polls Purchase status for the committed result. A late success must follow the defined expiry or compensation policy.

sections.title: 1) Contention
points: One shared inventory row serializes all reservations. More Sale Service instances do not remove that database bottleneck.
Redis can atomically update a counter and reservation through a script. It is then authoritative state, with durability and reconciliation responsibilities.
The preferred design stores one ReservationUnit row per available unit. A transaction selects a row with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
That transaction deletes the selected unit and creates the Reservation. Independent rows spread contention while both records stay in one database.
A temporary shortage of unlocked rows needs controlled retry behavior. Admission limits still protect the total database capacity.

flows.title: Claim an independent inventory unit
steps: The Sale Service starts a PostgreSQL transaction for the reservation request.
It selects an available ReservationUnit using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
It deletes that selected unit and inserts the buyer's Reservation within the same transaction.
It commits the claim and returns the reservation. Other requests can claim different unlocked units concurrently.
If no eligible unit is found, use the defined retry or expired-reservation path before reporting definitive unavailability.

sections.title: 2) Expiration
points: SQS delayed messages or durable timers can schedule expiry. Workers must recheck reservation state because jobs can run late or repeat.
The final design instead reclaims expired reservations when the available pool is empty. One short transaction claims a batch of expired units.
The reclaiming request keeps one unit and returns the others to the pool. A per-product lock prevents many requests from repeating this work.
Only active, expired claims can be reclaimed. Purchased claims and newer reservations must remain unchanged by delayed cleanup.

flows.title: Expire a reservation with a delayed job
steps: Reservation creation schedules a durable SQS message for its expiry time.
After the delay, a worker receives the reservation ID.
A short transaction verifies that the reservation remains active and has expired.
The transaction marks it expired and returns its unit to the available pool.
A repeated message or already purchased reservation changes nothing. This approach still depends on the worker running promptly.

flows.title: Reclaim expired inventory on demand
steps: A buyer's request finds no available ReservationUnit.
One request acquires the product's reclamation lock; competing requests wait briefly or retry the normal claim path.
A short transaction selects active reservations whose expiry has passed and marks them expired.
The request keeps one recovered unit for its new reservation and returns the remaining units to the available pool.
The transaction commits and releases the lock. Subsequent buyers spread across the available rows.

sections.title: 3) Crowd admission
points: A gateway rate limit protects storage but can cause repeated client retries. A waiting room gives users a controlled admission path.
The Waiting Room Service stores entries in Redis. An admission controller issues short-lived signed tokens at a rate the backend can sustain.
The API Gateway checks the token before forwarding a reservation request. Admitted users still compete for available inventory.
Scale waiting-room polling separately from reservations. If Redis state is sharded, the admission order must remain global.

flows.title: Admit waiting buyers at a sustainable rate
steps: The client joins the Waiting Room Service, which stores its queue entry in Redis.
The client checks its waiting status while the admission controller follows the chosen global order.
The controller admits users at a rate that leaves capacity for reservation transactions.
An admitted user receives a short-lived signed admission token.
The API Gateway validates the token before forwarding the reservation request to the Sale Service.
Admission grants permission to try. Only a committed reservation grants a temporary inventory claim.

sections.title: 4) Fairness
points: Randomize users already waiting when the sale starts. Users who arrive afterward join in arrival order.
Allow one active queue entry per authenticated user for the sale. A bot challenge can make automated mass entry harder.
Signed admission tokens prevent direct bypass of the waiting room. Fast inventory claims alone do not make access fair.

sections.title: Final Design
points: The Waiting Room Service controls arrivals at the Sale Service. PostgreSQL transactions claim independent ReservationUnit rows.
On-demand reclamation recovers expired units when the pool is empty. State checks prevent stale checkout or cleanup from changing a newer claim.
Stripe handles payment collection. Verified webhooks and conditional purchase updates preserve the inventory rule across delayed or repeated messages.
